articles.title: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech
articles.summary: Proposed changes could lead to new digital wallets and keys as well as ticketing apps, the regulator says.
articles.body:
UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower".

It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall.

Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation.

Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK.

In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets.

"This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards".

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals.

However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches.

The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK.

The UK is one of the world's leading fintech hubs, the CMA said, generating more than £214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs.

But Apple's fees and rules contactless payments are restricting growth and innovation, it argued.

Changes could enable the development of a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys, it claimed.

The regulator said moves to open up the tech in the EU had resulted in the creation of new businesses.

In the six months since the EU forced Apple to widen access to its tech, an alternative payment app Vipps launched, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA.

Apple argues however that the these new apps could easily have been launched prior to the changes.

But in the UK not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple's the watchdog argued.

The CMA said it was not proposing to set the price and terms Apple could demand for use of its devices contactless tech, but the effect of its plans would be that prices would fall.

Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA said it had been told that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology made it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.

"By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services," she said.

articles.title: Iran denies collapse is close as US claims IRGC running out of money
articles.summary: Iranian authorities defiant despite financial strain, saying they want to lift US blockade and pressure on their terms.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have rejected claims that Iran is unable to support its regional allies, but acknowledged that the United States’ sanctions and the war have created financial challenges.

US Central Command chief Brad Cooper claimed last week that a combination of military attacks and a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports “has dealt severe blows” to the country.

The admiral said the US had prevented at least $25bn in Iranian crude exports and helped freeze approximately $350m in cryptocurrency assets. This means the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are now unable to pay their soldiers and Iran-linked regional groups suffering from financial shortfalls.

“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also is not paying its troops,” Cooper said.

This is being portrayed as a victory for the US in its war with Iran, which so far has shown very few tangible victories for Washington.

Michael Knights, head of MENA research at US-based intelligence and geopolitical risk advisory firm Horizon Engage, said Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen have suffered financially during the past few years.

“The national economies feeding the Hezbollah and Houthi movements are badly broken, so they continue to receive stipends and in-kind funding – in fuel products – from Iran,” Knights told Al Jazeera.

For decades, the IRGC Quds Force has supplied money, weapons, components, training and manufacturing expertise to regional allied groups. It has enabled partners at loggerheads with the US and Israel to assemble or produce a number of weapons locally, according to United Nations experts and US officials.

The axis groups also draw on businesses, including oil exports, as well as donations and local resources to fund their operations. Some Iraqi factions have been integrated into the official security forces and receive government funding through the Popular Mobilisation Forces.

Allied commercial networks in Iraq are selling Iranian commodities and distributing proceeds through intermediaries and exchange houses, the US Department of the Treasury has claimed.

This has put them in a better financial position than their “poorer cousins” in Hezbollah and the Houthis, Knights said, with some money allegedly flowing from Iraq towards Iran in recent years.

“Some Iraqi militiamen and government civil servants are indeed paid late at the same time that Iraqi militias send funding overseas to help Iran, the Houthis and Lebanese Hezbollah,” he told Al Jazeera.

The US Treasury alleged in September that Kataib Hezbollah , a prominent Tehran-backed Shia Muslim armed group in neighbouring Iraq, siphoned Iraqi resources to support Iran.

The Treasury also described substantial earlier transfers from the Quds Force to Hezbollah, depicting flows in both directions.

A report by the Reuters news agency earlier this month cited unnamed sources as saying Hezbollah received $200m from Iran in September . The US State Department rejected the report at the time, saying Hezbollah was “trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran”.

Iran’s economy has taken hit after hit in recent years due to war, domestic mismanagement and sanctions .

This has led to runaway inflation, low-paying jobs, a depreciating national currency and isolation from the global community for 90 million Iranians.

There appears to be little sign of the situation improving, with the World Bank reporting earlier this month a projected 7.7 percent contraction of the economy in the fiscal year 2026-27.

The authorities emphasise that does not affect their resolve. They have also challenged US Treasury assessments that economic pressure could result in losing control within months .

“Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said earlier this month.

President Masoud Pezeshkian acknowledged on Sunday that military attacks and the maritime blockade had created substantial problems for the country. But he said his government was relying on domestic capacities to withstand the pressure.

He claimed consumption management had now removed the need for petrol imports that would otherwise cost $12bn, if US pressure allowed imports at all. The president promised to return revenues from recently increased fuel prices to households by modestly increasing their electronic food vouchers.

Knights said the Iranian authorities were “stuck in an aggressive cycle of escalation with the US government no matter what state Iran’s economy is in”.

“Trump is betting that being poorer will make Iran’s regime more flexible, but that has never been a good bet,” he said.

Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, said she expected Tehran to continue prioritising its regional allied groups despite the financial strains involved.

“Economic pressure is certainly constraining Iran’s military resources, but that does not mean it will fundamentally change the IRGC’s strategic calculations or force Tehran to surrender,” she told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: In 1933, Woolworth heiress Barbara Hutton ordered a Rolls-Royce for a Georgian prince; he died crashing that car, but it survived, crossed the Atlantic aboard the QE2 and sold for £166,750 in 2026
articles.summary: A luxury car built as a wedding gift became the centre of a remarkable story involving an American heiress, a Georgian prince, a fatal crash and a
articles.body: A luxury car built as a wedding gift became the centre of a remarkable story involving an American heiress, a Georgian prince, a fatal crash and a transatlantic journey. The 1933 Rolls-Royce Phantom II Continental Drophead Coupé, commissioned by Woolworth heiress Barbara Hutton for her first husband, Prince Alexis Mdivani, survived its owner's death and went on to cross the Atlantic aboard the Queen Elizabeth 2. More than nine decades after its construction, the historic motor car sold for £166,750, including the buyer's premium, at a Bonhams auction on September 19, 2026. According to Bonhams' auction catalogue, its rarity, bespoke engineering and documented history made it an especially distinctive example of pre-war automotive craftsmanship.A Rolls-Royce commissioned for a royal romanceBarbara Hutton, granddaughter of F. W. Woolworth, the founder of the Woolworth retail fortune, was among the world's wealthiest women by the age of 21. Often described in the press as the “Poor Little Rich Girl”, she became known for her lavish lifestyle and turbulent personal life. In the early 1930s, Hutton became engaged to Prince Alexis Mdivani, a Georgian aristocrat living in exile in Paris. To celebrate their forthcoming marriage, she commissioned a Rolls-Royce Phantom II Continental, chassis number 3MW, as a special gift for him.The car was built by Rolls-Royce with coachwork from the London-based firm Thrupp & Maberly. It was one of only three Phantom II Continental models to receive the company's distinctive Sedanca Drophead Coupé bodywork. The vehicle was displayed at the 1933 Paris Salon before delivery, placing it among the notable luxury cars showcased during the period.Inside the prince's aviation-inspired carThe Phantom II Continental was designed for more spirited touring than the standard Phantom II. Its shorter wheelbase and revised engineering offered improved performance, while its bespoke bodywork gave it a distinctive profile. Prince Mdivani, a qualified pilot, influenced several of the car's unusual specifications. The bonnet was extended by four inches, the bonnet louvres were angled at 13.5 degrees, and a larger 28-gallon fuel tank was fitted.The cabin was particularly distinctive. Turned aluminium panels featured across the interior, including the dashboard, which carried a specially ordered six-inch speedometer and tachometer. An altimeter and variometer, instruments associated with aviation, added to the aircraft-inspired design. Adjustable hydraulic shock absorbers also allowed the suspension to be stiffened for high-speed driving. These details made the vehicle more than a conventional luxury car, reflecting its owner's interests and the era's fascination with speed and technological innovation.A fatal crash, followed by a second lifeHutton and Mdivani reportedly took the Rolls-Royce on their honeymoon. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1935, with Mdivani retaining the car. Shortly afterwards, while holidaying in Spain, the prince was driving at high speed when he crashed the vehicle and was killed. The car survived the accident and was returned to Hutton.According to Bonhams, Hutton is understood to have sent it back to Rolls-Royce and Thrupp & Maberly for a comprehensive refurbishment. It subsequently passed through several British owners and underwent restoration by FLM Panelcraft during the 1950s or 1960s. Its history then took it across the Atlantic. In the mid-1970s, the car travelled to the United States aboard the Cunard liner Queen Elizabeth 2, commonly known as the QE2.It remained in American ownership for decades and reportedly received careful maintenance, including an engine rebuild attributed to Rolls-Royce enthusiast Frank Cook. After nearly 50 years with a single owner, it passed to another custodian in 2018.The historic car sells for £166,750The Rolls-Royce was acquired by its most recent seller at a US auction in 2023. It was subsequently sent to Restocar SA, specialists in pre-war cars based in Clarens, Switzerland, for comprehensive servicing, with an invoice of CHF 18,000 included in the car's history file. Bonhams offered the vehicle as Lot 231 at its Goodwood Revival Collectors' Motor Cars and Automobilia sale on September 19, 2026. The car sold for £166,750, including the buyer's premium. Its appeal lay in the combination of rarity, bespoke construction and an unusually well-documented ownership history. The auction listing also included copies of factory build records and described the car as an older restoration.From a commission celebrating a royal romance to a fatal accident and a voyage aboard one of the world's best-known ocean liners, the Phantom II Continental has survived a succession of extraordinary chapters. Its 2026 sale marked another milestone in the life of a car whose significance extends beyond its luxurious design to the people and events associated with it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
articles.summary: Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets.

Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis.

The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital.

Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal.

So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery?

After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd).

Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”.

“[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said.

The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company.

The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone.

Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products.

Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”.

The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade.

Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday.

Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies?

Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods.

Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month.

Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes.

Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura.

The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland.

CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude. The Jamnagar refinery is a prime example of that loophole.

Rubio’s visit to the refinery also comes as Trump faces his worst approval ratings amid inflation and rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in November. Just about 31 percent of Americans are happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever number in his two terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey.

The Trump administration has also reportedly been pushing Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian energy facilities, which have rattled the global fuel markets.

Why the refinery is important for the Russia-Ukraine war

Reliance is also a critical actor in US efforts to influence how much oil Russia sells.

Since the start of Russia’s full-fledged war on Ukraine in February 2022, India has emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. And Reliance is driving that surge in imports. While only 3 percent of its oil was sourced from Russia before 2022, that share rose to 50 percent by 2025.

So when Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to punish New Delhi for the purchase of Russian oil, Reliance was directly affected. It cut back on Russian crude imports significantly in subsequent months, but it still made up a third of the oil processed by Jamnagar’s refinery during the July-September 2026 quarter.

That was under threat when the Trump administration appeared poised to impose a 100 percent tariff on Indian goods because of continued Russian oil imports, under a new law passed last month.

But Trump has since suspended those proposed tariffs, easing concerns for India and Reliance.

Rubio has said India has been diversifying its import mix away from Russian crude, even as it still buys millions of barrels of Russian oil every day. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” Rubio said on Sunday.

“But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”

Yes, India’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, is investing in the US, primarily through energy-related projects.

It is backing America First Refining’s planned oil refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas, also the first major US refinery in about 50 years, announced by Trump in March.

The refinery is expected to cost $3bn to $4bn and process about 60 million barrels of US crude annually. Reliance has signed a 20-year agreement to buy a large share of the facility’s output, with operations expected to start around 2029.

In November 2024, Reliance’s US subsidiary also acquired a 21 percent stake in helium explorer Wavetech Helium for $12m as part of its low-carbon energy strategy.

Last month, Trump announced that India’s Essar Group — an oil major with knee-deep ties to Russia — is planning an $18bn integrated steel investment in the US through its subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics.

Didn’t Trump’s ally just lock horns with Ambani?

Despite Reliance’s investments in the US and Rubio’s upcoming visit to the Jamnagar facility, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who is also a key Trump ally, recently hit out at Ambani.

His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.

In ⁠a series of X posts recently, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to ⁠favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio. Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing ‌him as “Prime ‌Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.

In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

articles.title: Andy Burnham risks wrath of Commons Speaker for talking too much at PMQs
articles.summary: The prime minister takes longer than his predecessors to respond to questions from MPs, writes Matt Chorley.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has only been prime minister for three months, but he is already in trouble with the Commons Speaker for talking too much.

During the first three sessions of Prime Minister's Questions with Burnham at the despatch box, Sir Lindsay Hoyle has made repeated appeals for brevity.

But is he really any more verbose than his predecessors like Sir Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson?

Armed with a stopwatch for a dive into the archive, I've found that the new prime minister does seem to give fuller, longer answers – by some margin.

The weekly session of PMQs is scheduled to start at midday on Wednesdays when the Commons is sitting, and last for 30 minutes. However it routinely runs for 10, 15, even 20 minutes longer. And that has caused problems.

Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics

" Can I just say I admire the prime minister?" Sir Lindsay said during Burnham's first PMQs.

"At least he's answering detailed questions. My problem is I'm not going to get through the list, and both of us will be in trouble with the backbenches when we don't make it."

Just last week he complained again: "We really are going to have to try and speed up some of the answers."

Based on an average of his first three times taking PMQs, Burnham has spoken for a total of 22 minutes per session. That's between three and six minutes more than the average for the other PMs I looked at each over three similar autumn sessions.

The number of questions asked each week can differ though, in part because time is running out. So I looked at the average time spent on each answer

Of those I looked at, Truss was the fastest - averaging just 33 seconds per answer, followed by Johnson on 35 seconds, Sir Keir on 38 seconds and Sunak on 39 seconds.

By contrast Burnham was an outlier, taking on average 51 seconds per answer.

That means he talks for a third more per question than Sir Keir and Sunak, and up to 50% more than Truss.

Obviously the quantity of words is easier to assess than the quality.

Number 10 thinks there is a simple reason why the current PM takes longer than his predecessors. A senior source tells me: "It's because he actually answers the questions."

A spokesman for the speaker said: "The speaker is always keen to get in as many backbenchers as possible for any question session."

Listen to Matt Chorley weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live and on the Urgent Questions podcast .

articles.title: Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch
articles.summary: Speaking ahead of next week's Budget, the Conservative leader says her party would make £70bn of cuts.
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said Labour will not have the "courage" to make the public spending cuts she argued were necessary to bring down debt and fund defence.

Speaking in central London, the Conservative leader said the chancellor was hoping to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" next week but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."

Highlighting her own plans to reduce spending by £70bn, Badenoch said: "Cuts are never easy but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described Badenoch's solution as "reverse Robin Hood politics – giving tax breaks to the wealthiest while offering nothing to ordinary people".

Chancellor John Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans on 28 October - the first Budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Healey has come under pressure to set out how he will boost defence funding to 3% of national income by 2030. However, this announcement is not expected until the government's spending review next year.

The Budget is also unlikely to include details about any changes to the welfare system, with those expected once former cabinet minister Alan Milburn produces his review into young people and work.

Badenoch said: "If Labour's plan is to kick tough decisions into the long grass, come out with tiny bits of micro-policy, put up a few taxes, spend a bit more on welfare, and hope nobody notices before the next election, they are kidding themselves."

The Tory leader noted that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had recently praised the UK for its plans to reduce its borrowing.

"The IMF clearly don't know this Labour Party like I do," she said.

She said Labour's plans required "huge cuts to the public sector" in 2029 and that the party would call an election before then.

"They are not suddenly going to find the courage to cut spending in the final year of a Parliament right before an election... Investors aren't buying these fictional cuts either."

Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor

Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

The most recent figures show that in August government borrowing stood at £18.3bn. The government is paying £8.8bn on its debt - the highest level since records began in 1997.

Badenoch said her party would reduce borrowing by finding £70bn of savings, including through cuts to the welfare bill.

Under her party's "golden economic rule", half of the savings would go towards reducing the deficit.

"Cuts are never easy, but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair," she said.

"Fair to taxpayers, fair to future generations, and fair to those who really do need support."

The Conservatives have recently announced they would scrap inheritance tax on family homes and allow couples to leave £1m tax-free.

Asked if the Conservatives were the party for the rich, Badenoch told the BBC her policies would "help everyone".

"Quite frankly, getting people off welfare is doing something for them... the best welfare is a well-paying job," she said.

Pressed on whether she would make changes to the triple lock to reduce the amount spent on pensions, Badenoch said she did not want to see "pensioner poverty" and that there were other things the party could do to grow the economy.

The trade unions and the Liberal Democrats have urged the government to raise money by putting a windfall tax on banks, who have reported large profits in recent years.

Badenoch dismissed this suggestion, arguing it would hit bank shareholders, including people's pension funds.

Setting out her party's policy Liberal Democrat leader Daisy Cooper said: "It's outrageous that while households have been grappling with the cost-of-living crisis, the big banks have benefited from a taxpayer-funded windfall worth billions."

She said the money raised from putting higher taxes on the bank could go towards reducing the cost of petrol and diesel and transport fares.

Reform UK economic spokesman Robert Jenrick challenged Healey to use the Budget to increase funding for defence, reduce benefit fraud and to make cuts to "foreign aid to rich countries" and "all the mad net-zero subsidies".

Speaking at a Reform rally in Plymouth, Jenrick added: "I suspect he won't. In fact, I confidently predict that this Budget will contain exactly what the last two did: tax rises again."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, Phillipson said: "Under the Tories debt rocketed, interest rates went up, while family finances and businesses were hammered.

"Labour has taken the fair decisions to reverse the Conservatives' decline. The economy is growing, interest rates have fallen, and private investment has returned.

"We're giving people breathing space on the cost of living and delivering everyday fixes to make life that little bit easier."

articles.title: Harry says he wants to 'reconcile' with his family
articles.summary: Prince Harry says he wants reconciliation with his family, in an interview with a magazine in New York last month.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex has said he wants to repair his complicated relationships with his father and brother, in a magazine interview.

"Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York.

"Scars stick around forever. But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past, that's something that I would encourage everybody to do," said Prince Harry.

Last week Prince Harry and Meghan carried out their first public engagement together since their return to the UK in the summer.

The GQ interview with Prince Harry was conducted last month and released as the Royal Family were on duty in Windsor welcoming the Sultan of Oman at the start of a state visit.

But a spokesman for the Sussexes said the interview was recorded in late September and it was the entirely the publishers' decision when to run it - and that nothing should be read into the timing.

The spokesman also said that the reference to "some people don't want it to work out" was not a swipe at his brother Prince William or any other member of his family.

Prince Harry and Meghan moved from the UK to the United States in 2020, stepping down as working royals in what was an acrimonious departure.

Harry's memoir, Spare, showed the depth of the family fall out and the damaged relationship with his brother William.

Despite Prince Harry now being physically nearer to his family in the UK, there hasn't seemed to be any more emotional closeness with his brother Prince William, and in this interview Harry seems to be open to reconciliation.

It was a message of wanting to build bridges that he had previously sent in a BBC interview in May 2025, when he had been living in the US.

Prince Harry recognised that this royal story of family disagreements fascinated the public, saying it was "massively relatable".

"Sibling disagreements, broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent - that continues to come up with me the whole time with people that I speak to," he said.

Asked by GQ about the reason for his move back to the UK, Prince Harry said: "Opportunities for the family. Being able to put the kids in a British school has meant a lot to me. I didn't know how important it was to me."

"They [Archie and Lilibet] are loving it, and it's just giving them a whole different experience."

He told the magazine: "To be back, closer to my family, and to be back on UK soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there".

Prince Harry also reflects on the King's health, following his treatment for cancer, saying: "He's getting better".

There were also comments about growing up with a sense of loss after the death of his mother, Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997.

"I love the fact that I'm able to now sort of carry the memory of my mother with me, with my work, rather than it hold me down, pull me back, or wallowing in that grief," he said.

He rejected any sense of wanting public sympathy.

"I certainly don't want any sympathy. That's where we're way past that. Why? Because I'm a prince. I've got a support network around me, I've done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work. I wonder where I would be if I didn't - it could be a very different situation," he said.

articles.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 200 people, sources say
articles.summary: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
articles.body:
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 200 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 73 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.

A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.

The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.

South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.

Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.

The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.

"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday .

The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.

Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line

The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.

A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.

Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.

Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.

Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.

The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) and had killed 73 people, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.

"We were surprised by bombing and thick smoke inside Amiet Common Market, which is located 10km [six miles] from Abyei town," he said.

BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.

It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.

Ngor told the Reuters news agency that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.

Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.

"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.

Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.

It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.

Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

articles.title: Pakistan army chief in Tehran: Can diplomacy prevent new US-Iran fighting?
articles.summary: With new talk of escalation, Islamabad is trying to revive negotiations without alienating Tehran, Riyadh or Washington.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s army chief , Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday evening for talks with Iranian officials, as diplomatic efforts ramp up to prevent a new round of fighting with the United States and Israel.

Munir’s visit is his fifth to Iran since the April ceasefire between Tehran and Washington, which was brokered by Islamabad. Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi is accompanying Munir, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported. The Pakistani army chief is expected to meet Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi first, IRNA said.

The visit comes a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks in Tehran, and two weeks after Pakistan and its allies agreed to accelerate the deployment of forces to Saudi Arabia, which has come under repeated attacks from the Iran-backed Houthi armed group in Yemen.

Lavrov’s visit on Monday was his first to Tehran since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February. The Russian foreign minister met Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian, and the talks covered the war, the Strait of Hormuz and efforts to end the fighting.

“The timing of [Munir’s] visit, following Lavrov’s presence in Tehran, suggests that Iran prefers to keep multiple diplomatic channels open, rather than relying exclusively on a single mediator,” Seyed Mojtaba Jalazadeh, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, told Al Jazeera.

But the Munir visit also comes at a time when some experts have warned of growing signs that United States President Donald Trump might be preparing for a return to fighting with Iran. Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war on September 26. Since then, the US has deployed an additional aircraft carrier to the Middle East, which is expected to arrive by late November. Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel’s upcoming October 27 election, referring to their shared mission in attacking Iran. Trump said that if Netanyahu were not re-elected, the US would need to attack Iran on its own.

Analysts say these developments add urgency to diplomatic efforts to sidestep a potential military escalation. In recent weeks, Qatar has played a key role in channeling proposals between the US and Iran. Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that while Qatar increasingly provides the diplomatic machinery behind the talks, Doha still values Islamabad’s access to Washington and Tehran.

“Pakistan offers political access, particularly through Field Marshal Asim Munir, while Qatar does much of the detailed negotiating,” Krieg said.

Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel began striking Iran on February 28.

Islamabad brokered a ceasefire on April 8 and, days later, hosted the highest-level direct engagement between the US and Iran since 1979.

In June, the two sides agreed to a 14-point memorandum of understanding (MoU).

Under the agreement, the US was to lift its naval blockade within 30 days, the Strait of Hormuz was to reopen, and about $24bn in estimated frozen Iranian assets was to be released in phases over 60 days of further talks, including negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

That period expired in mid-August without either side agreeing to extend it. Iran says the US failed to meet its commitments, and Tehran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, insisting that Washington first lift the blockade.

Pakistan’s Foreign Office has continued to point to the agreement and its utility.

“The Islamabad MoU is already in place, and some of the points currently under discussion are fully aligned with it,” spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan told a weekly briefing on October 9.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on October 2 that Iran’s seven-day plan was drawn from the MoU.

Analysts, however, disagree on whether the agreement can still provide a basis for negotiations.

“On the Islamabad MoU, I think it’s done from both sides and perhaps a new mechanism is required to start negotiations,” Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, told Al Jazeera.

Krieg said that while the Islamabad MoU was “politically alive”, it was “operationally dead”.

“The circumstances under which it was signed have fundamentally changed,” he said.

But Muhammad Faisal, a South Asia security researcher at the University of Technology Sydney, said the agreement could still be used.

“The Islamabad MoU remains usable, even if the political and security environment has deteriorated,” he told Al Jazeera. “It is still the minimum agreed benchmark between Washington and Tehran, and neither side has an obvious alternative framework for addressing the issues related to maritime access, sanctions relief and nuclear talks.”

Meanwhile, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7.

It was Pakistan’s second defence pact with Saudi Arabia, after the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement the two countries signed in September 2025.

At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on October 5, the three countries agreed to expedite the deployment of forces and capabilities under the pact.

Within days, Houthi missiles and drones struck Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport more than once, as well as targets in Abha, Yanbu and Shaybah.

Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, the Pakistani military’s spokesman, discussed the defence pact and the importance of protecting holy sites in Mecca and Medina in an interview with Independent Arabia on October 18.

“The security of the Harmain Sharifain is paramount. It’s non-negotiable,” he said, referring to Islam’s two holiest mosques. “Whatever support is needed to do that is being provided and will be provided.”

He declined to provide details, citing operational confidentiality.

Chaudhry said Pakistan wanted a negotiated end to the conflict. “If we are unable to come to a negotiated outcome and we turn into a military conflict, then this collective deterrence, this instrument of collective deterrence of Mecca Alliance will definitely come into play, as it is coming into play,” he said.

Asked at the October 9 briefing whether Pakistani forces in Saudi Arabia would engage the Houthis, Foreign Office spokesman Khan said they would not.

“These forces would not cross the border into Yemen to launch attacks against the Houthis,” he said.

On Monday, a day before leaving for Tehran, Munir met Saudi ambassador to Pakistan, Rajeh Tami Albugamy. A statement said the two expressed satisfaction with progress under the pact, but made no mention of the Houthis or Iran.

Tehran’s public response to the agreement has largely been restrained. On October 11, Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart , Prince Faisal bin Farhan, that Tehran was ready to provide “any possible assistance” to start a dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, IRNA reported.

Saudi state media said that the two only discussed the “recent escalation in violence in the region”.

After meeting Iranian leaders in New York last month, Dar said they had told him Iran had nothing to do with the Houthis and had suggested engaging them politically rather than militarily.

But Krieg said Pakistan’s two roles were becoming harder to reconcile.

“Pakistan remains an important intermediary, but its credibility as a neutral actor is increasingly compromised by its security commitments to Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Jalazadeh said Tehran’s concern was more limited.

“Iran does not necessarily perceive stronger defence cooperation between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia as an immediate threat, but it does regard it as a complicating and constraining factor,” he said.

But it’s not just Pakistan facing competing pressures — or sending seemingly mixed signals.

In Washington, Trump has pledged not to strike Iran before the US midterm elections.

“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the US on November 3rd,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform on October 8. In the same post, he said the US was having productive discussions with Iran. The naval blockade has remained in place.

Ten days later, though, Trump endorsed Netanyahu. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.

On Monday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Netanyahu at Ovda airbase in southern Israel during an unannounced visit, Axios reported. The outlet said the visit came amid US-Israeli discussions about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran.

“Threats of military strikes, combined with the blockade and indirect negotiations, undermine Iran’s confidence in Washington’s intentions and make stronger security guarantees one of the central issues in any potential agreement,” Jalazadeh said.

Faisal told Al Jazeera that the timing of the two votes, a week apart, made major concessions difficult for both sides and raised the risk of escalation.

Krieg said the elections were among the strongest constraints on another major war, but warned that the risk could grow once they had passed.

“The immediate danger is that Iran overplays its hand,” he said. “A major attack causing American casualties could override electoral calculations altogether.”

articles.title: Alberta rejects separation referendum: What’s next for Canadian province?
articles.summary: Calls for independence intensified last year, with some 300,000 petitioning officials for a referendum.
articles.body:
Voters in Alberta have chosen to remain part of Canada in a first-ever independence referendum.

Canadian state broadcaster CBC News called the results of Monday’s vote late on the same day after 48 percent of the ballots counted showed overwhelming support for the “remain” side, with 76 percent opting to stay with Canada.

The result marks a major win for Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is facing a trade and political war with the United States amid US President Donald Trump’s higher tariffs and repeated suggestions of annexing the country.

On his way into a cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning, Carney called it a “great day.”

“I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose,” he said.

But the result also comes as a disappointment for those Albertans seeking independence for the resource-rich region following years of grievances laid at Ottawa’s door.

And while the vote represents a decisive rejection of separation, it may not spell the end for a movement that has spent decades pushing for greater autonomy from the federal government.

The nonbinding referendum was first announced in May following a campaign and petition by a group of Albertans who want to be an independent country.

While only about one-third of Albertans were found to be pro-independence in polls, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith argued in her announcement that a referendum was necessary to respect the 300,000 Albertans who had petitioned officials for it.

In the referendum, voters answered 10 questions, including whether the government should begin a binding process to seek independence from Canada. They also answered questions on immigration, access to provincial services like education, social care and healthcare, and voter identification requirements.

But even if voters had chosen to pursue independence, Alberta would not have automatically separated from Canada. A win for the independence side in a subsequent referendum would have set the stage for complex negotiations between Alberta, the federal government, the other provinces and Indigenous peoples.

Prime Minister Carney had campaigned for Albertans to vote “remain”, saying last week at a rally in Calgary that separation would be “ a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division”.

“There are some outside our borders who are working to break us so they can own us,” he said.

Researchers have pointed to possible online influence campaigns by both Russian and US entities that helped amplify the call for separation and allegedly shared misleading information. Alberta PM Smith told media in August that the online activity was under observation.

Prime Minister Carney, who grew up in the region, said “Albertans made a clear choice” in a statement he made early on Tuesday.

“They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he said, adding that “Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition.”

Alberta’s Premier Smith said she was pleased to see the results and that “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.”

While Smith opposed independence, her decision to hold the referendum gave separatists an opportunity to put their cause in front of voters across the province.

Smith had encouraged voters to vote in favour of the nine other questions on the ballot, which touched on issues like immigration and judicial appointments. Preliminary results showed voters had chosen to support eight of nine of those measures.

The rejection of separation could now allow her government to shift its focus back to demands on those issues and its broader push for greater autonomy for Alberta within Canada.

But separatist leaders made clear they had no intension of abandoning their cause.

At a gathering to watch the results in Edmonton, Jeffrey Rath, a leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters the push for independence would “absolutely continue.”

“We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re continuing to move forward.”

Cory Morgan, founder of the separatist group Pathway to Independence, wrote on X that “a great base of support for independence has been fostered which isn’t going away,” and called supporters to continue working towards separation.

First Nations groups turned out in strong numbers to vote to remain with Canada, with one southern Alberta polling station in an area home to the Siksika Nation temporarily running out of ballots, local media reported.

Why is Alberta important, and why are there calls for independence?

Many Albertans have long complained that their critical natural resources are funding the government in Ottawa and the commercial hubs of Toronto and Montreal, but that the province does not receive proportionate benefits.

The province, with a population of 5.1 million, holds massive oil deposits. It also holds reserves of critical and rare-earth metals including lithium, titanium and zircon, which are essential for manufacturing many tech items, from smartphones to fighter jets.

Separatist movements, some of which even support Alberta joining the US, go back to the 1940s, following the discovery of oil reserves. Some of Alberta’s premiers have had spats with Ottawa over wealth distribution.

US President Trump has made remarks about Canada becoming a US state in recent months.

Last week, he told a political rally in the US state of Arizona that Canada will “end up being the 51st state, because it’s the only way it works”.

The two countries have been embroiled in a trade war since talks fell apart in August this year and they slapped each other with tit-for-tat tariffs.

Earlier this month, tech billionaire Elon Musk called for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec to separate from Canada, saying “they’d be better off”.

But the matter of Alberta’s independence gained intense scrutiny last year after pro-separatists launched a petition to pressure the government.

Alberta, alongside other western provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, have all complained about “western alienation” by the government in the centre.

Is it over for Alberta’s independence bid?

With separatism agitations running so far back, experts say the referendum will likely not end the movement altogether.

Ahead of the vote, some separatist leaders said they would pursue another referendum if necessary, arguing that the referendum shows that independence is legally possible.

Cory Morgan, founder of the advocacy group Pathway to Independence, said the result did not mean the end of the movement.

“A great base of support for independence has been fostered which isn’t going away,” he wrote on X, calling on supporters to continue working towards separation.

articles.body: El liderazgo día a día de MARCA.com en los medios digitales españoles sigue siendo indiscutible. Nuestro sitio web es el más leído de España a diario tanto en los medios deportivos como generalistas, según el informe correspondiente al mes de septiembre elaborado por GfK, el medidor oficial de audiencias digitales del país, que sitúa a MARCA al frente en todas las métricas de calidad. Con una audiencia media diaria de 3.411.293 usuarios, MARCA se impone tanto a medios generalistas como deportivos. No hay ningún medio en España que supere la barrera de los tres millones de lectores diarios. Por detrás se sitúan As, que alcanza los 2.561.515 y El Español con 2.277.886 y El País con 2.144.811. Es significativo que de todos los medios deportivos el único que sigue creciendo con respecto al mes pasado fue MARCA (+4,3%) frente a los descensos de As (-3,4%), Mundo Deportivo (-4,6%) y Sport (-16,3%). El liderazgo de MARCA también se refleja en el volumen total de consumo durante el mes de septiembre, rozando los mil millones de páginas vistas (910.691.490). A gran distancia aparece As, segundo en este apartado con 493.614.236. Asimismo, MARCA destaca en otra de las métricas clave: la tasa de rebote. El medio deportivo de referencia en castellano en todo el mundo registra el menor porcentaje del mercado, con un 39%, lo que evidencia el alto nivel de interés y permanencia de los usuarios. En comparación, sus principales seguidores presentan cifras notablemente superiores: As alcanza el 54%, Mundo Deportivo el 58% y Sport el 52%. En sesiones, MARCA.com arrasa a sus competidores con sus 395 millones, casi el doble que As (195) y muy por delante de MD (92) y Sport (54). En redes sociales, MARCA reafirma un mes más un dominio que ya se había acentuado en el verano con los resultados históricos en los meses de junio, julio y agosto con el Mundial de fútbol, donde alcanzó sus mejores registros en interacciones y visualizaciones de Instagram, Tiktok y Youtube, así como con el inicio de la Liga y la Champions. Durante el mes de septiembre, MARCA continúa con su liderazgo absoluto en España acercándose a los 30 millones de seguidores en todas sus plataformas sociales.

articles.title: Eastern Libya parliament approves 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye
articles.summary: The vote recognises Ankara’s maritime deal with Tripoli, ending Haftar’s 2020 boycott.
articles.body:
Libya’s eastern-based parliament, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, which runs as an alternative to the UN-recognised legislature in Tripoli, has approved a maritime deal with Turkiye, ending years of acrimony.

Haftar’s Benghazi-based government said in a statement on Tuesday that his Tobruk-based House of Representatives voted unanimously to approve the 2019 memorandum of understanding signed between Turkiye and Libya’s UN-recognised former Government of National Accord (GNA) on the delimitation of maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean Sea.

Specialised committees presented a full and detailed explanation of the deal’s provisions, lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told the Reuters news agency.

The approval came six years after the same parliament ⁠in 2020 unanimously rejected the ratification of the deal and cut political ties with Ankara.

The repealing of those moves on Tuesday consolidates a strategic shift in the works since last year, building on Ankara’s military-to-military contacts with Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), including a deal in July to develop military facilities and advanced surveillance systems.

The LNA, long believed to have been supported by Egypt and other regional powers, has been in conflict with forces loyal to the Tripoli-based government since the start of the Libyan civil war in 2014.

In 2019, Turkiye signed an agreement with the Tripoli-based government delineating the maritime boundaries between the two countries in the Mediterranean, triggering protests from Greece and Cyprus.

Reacting to the latest announcement on Tuesday, Greece’s Foreign Ministry said the ‌2019 memorandum violated international law of the sea and infringed on the sovereign rights of states in the region, calling on Libya to refrain from actions ⁠that undermine stability in ⁠the Mediterranean.

Athens said it had informed partners and allies and ‌would take all appropriate measures to safeguard its sovereign ‌rights.

Earlier, Tarek al-Jeroushi, a lawmaker in the eastern-backed parliament said “some countries may be upset by this ⁠agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest”. He added that the ⁠agreement would strengthen Libya’s position as a political, military and economic partner to key powers.

In December 2019, Haftar’s LNA had nearly encircled Tripoli, threatening to overrun the UN-recognised GNA, which at the time was led by Fayez al-Sarraj, before Turkiye decided to intervene, sending military advisers and drones to stop the LNA, and altering the trajectory of the Libyan civil war.

Seven years later, there is talk of Ankara setting up a military presence in areas under the control of Haftar’s LNA.

This eastern pivot is designed to secure Turkiye’s long-term geopolitical and economic interests, preserving its influence in Libya regardless of future political settlements between the government and eastern authorities.

articles.title: Trump admin revoked more than 300,000 visas since 2025, including 4,000 linked to birth tourism: Report
articles.summary: The Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 visas since January 2025, with at least 4,000 related to birth tourism, marking a record cancellation rate linked to immigration violations and national security concerns.
articles.body: The Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 visas since President Donald Trump returned to office in January last year, including at least 4,000 linked to people accused of engaging in or facilitating birth tourism, The New York Post reported.A State Department official told the newspaper that the visa cancellations were linked to criminal activity, threats to public safety and immigration violations, including fraud and misrepresentation.State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the administration had revoked visas at a faster rate than any previous administration.“With over 300,000 revocations, the Trump administration has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history,” Pigott said.He added that the administration would continue to take action against foreign nationals who violate the law or pose national security concerns while in the US on visas.The State Department has not immediately disclosed the nationalities of those whose visas were revoked, The New York Post reported.The latest figure marks an increase from last month, when the department confirmed that up to 250,000 visas had been revoked since January 2025. According to the report, about 25% of the visas cancelled that year involved assault or related crimes. articles.title: Former MIT scientist wins $6 million in sexual misconduct suit by younger female colleague, says predator tag damaged career while it was a consensual relationship
articles.summary: A Boston court exonerated former MIT scientist David Sabatini, 58, of sexual misconduct allegations brought by former colleague Kristin Knouse and asked
articles.body: A Boston court exonerated former MIT scientist David Sabatini, 58, of sexual misconduct allegations brought by former colleague Kristin Knouse and asked Knouse to pay Sabatini $6 million in damages. Sabatini lost his job after Knouse brought the allegations and claimed that Sabatini pressured her into a relationship starting in 2018 when they were both working at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, affiliated with MIT.Knouse said Sabatini created a sexualized and hostile environment in his laboratory. An internal investigation found Sabatini responsible for violating the institute's policy governing workplace relationships. He was removed from his post.Sabatini maintained that the relationship was consensual and it ended after he began pursuing another woman. Sabatini filed a lawsuit against the Whitehead Institute, and Knouse also brought a lawsuit against him alleging that he had abused his position of power.Knouse left in tears after verdictBoston Globe reported the courtroom scenes after the verdict was given. The Suffolk County jury sided with Sabatini and Knouse was ordered to pay $6 million plus interest. Knouse who is currently an assistant professor of biology at MIT and a faculty member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research, was left in tears. “It is disappointing that the jury’s verdict reflects none of this. It is sadly a marker of our times where it is still hard for women to be believed, and still hard to call powerful men to account,” Ellen Zucker, who represented Knouse in the case, told PEOPLE."She was not the only one who came to court to speak about what they had observed and encountered with Dr. Sabatini. There were multiple women who took the stand and talked about very concerning experiences they had in the course of their training in the Sabatini lab," Zucker said.Sabatini whose cancer research generated speculation that he could someday win a Nobel Prize said the allegations severely damaged his career. Sabatini’s attorney, Lisa Arrowood, called the verdict “a moment of sweet justice” for Sabatini, adding that her client’s life “was ruined” following Knouse’s claims. “After being branded a sexual harasser over five years ago, 13 Suffolk county jurors (seven women and six men) found that David Sabatini did not sexually harass Kristin Knouse and that she defamed him by calling him a sexual predator,” Arrowood told PEOPLE.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mary Berry’s daughter Belles Berry’s £3.95 million Oxfordshire mansion goes under offer; inside Blenheim Farm’s 10-acre estate with swimming pool, tennis court and over 4,000 sq ft of living space
articles.summary: Dame Mary Berry’s daughter, Belles Berry, has received an offer for her £3.95 million country mansion, Blenheim Farm, in South Oxfordshire.
articles.body: Dame Mary Berry’s daughter, Belles Berry, has received an offer for her £3.95 million country mansion, Blenheim Farm, in South Oxfordshire. The sprawling property, which features a swimming pool, tennis court, two kitchens and panoramic countryside views, is currently listed as “under offer” on Savills’ website.According to Oxford Mail, the property was put on the market in the spring with an asking price of £3,950,000. The estate agent’s website indicates that an offer has been accepted, with the parties working towards finalising the deal.Inside Belles Berry’s £3.95 million mansionLocated near the village of Ewelme, close to Wallingford, Blenheim Farm was designed and built by Belles and her husband in 2020 on the site of an old bungalow. Set amid 10 acres of South Oxfordshire countryside, the property offers more than 4,000 sq ft of accommodation.The bespoke home features floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors that provide views of the surrounding gardens and countryside. Its interiors combine colourful design elements with practical spaces for family life and entertaining.The handmade kitchen, dining and family room serves as the heart of the house. Designed by Belles, the kitchen features a central island, a two-metre champagne chiller and a dove-grey, five-door Aga gifted by her mother, Mary Berry. Antique painted wooden pews and a dresser sourced from a French monastery add character to the space.The property also has a second kitchen and utility room, allowing the family to keep cooking equipment separate from the main entertaining area.“The joy of designing your own house is you can have two dishwashers, two washing machines, two fridges and six bins if you want to – and we did,” Belles said.Library houses part of her father’s literary collectionThe mansion’s library features floor-to-ceiling bookshelves and a window overlooking the kitchen and the surrounding countryside. The room houses part of Belles’ father’s literary collection, which included more than 5,000 books from his antiquarian bookshop.A separate study serves as Belles’ creative space and houses her collection of cookery and gardening books.The principal bedroom features a copper bathtub positioned to take advantage of the views, along with a large dressing room and an en-suite bathroom. Moroccan-inspired interiors, including a fountain in the entrance hall, add to the property’s distinctive design.The house incorporates materials and finishes from several established brands, including Porcelanosa tiles, Lefroy Brooks bathroom fittings, Lazenby polished concrete flooring and bespoke wallpaper by Zigati, Gucci and Cole & Son.The media room features wallpaper by Andrew Martin and an original 1970s tan leather sofa, while some of the furniture comes from Belles’ father’s antiquarian bookshop.An oak-framed music room, which was converted into a games room during lockdown, provides another space for the family to spend time together.Swimming pool, tennis court and a three-bedroom cottageBeyond the main house, Blenheim Farm includes several additional features across its extensive grounds. The property has a swimming pool, a tennis court and a large shearing shed or barn that can accommodate cars or boats.There is also a characterful, three-bedroom barn-style cottage, which is currently let. It features an oak-framed, vaulted kitchen and sitting room, three en-suite bedrooms and a large loft that serves as additional reception space.The grounds include gardens designed by Clara Gardens, a fruit garden and a 60-year-old beech woodland. The family has also maintained the property’s agricultural character, with a large shearing shed that still displays alpaca rosettes.Belles and her family previously lived in the old bungalow on the site after moving to the property in 2014. Blenheim Farm was once an alpaca farm, and Belles described herself as an “accidental smallholder” after taking care of orphaned lambs, cows and ducks, as well as keeping bees.Belles Berry says designing the house was a dream projectSpeaking about the property, Belles revealed that she studied Feng Shui before the house was designed, paying close attention to the architectural layout and positioning of the rooms.“I studied Feng Shui before we designed the house; a lot of thought went into the architectural drawings and where everything should go,” she said.“We worked together with RPA Architects. It was a dream project and one we are extremely proud of.“It’s a happy house, and it has the wow factor, as the whole of one side is glass and south-facing.”Belles also recalled hosting her mother’s 80th birthday celebration in the property's shearing shed on a summer’s day. The rose garden features Chandos Beauty roses, one of Mary Berry’s favourites.Mary Berry’s close bond with her daughter’s familyBelles described Blenheim Farm as the perfect home for her family, recalling the time spent raising animals, tending the gardens and keeping bees.“Blenheim Farm has been the perfect home for the family.“The children had an idyllic time, I became an accidental smallholder and enjoyed rearing lambs, cows, ducks and beekeeping,” she said.She also shared a glimpse into her relationship with her mother, who lives with her husband, Paul Hunnings, in Henley-on-Thames, around six miles from Blenheim Farm.Belles said Mary regularly helped her pick and prune fruit in the garden. The family would collect blackcurrants and gooseberries, with Mary turning the harvest into homemade blackcurrant jam.“Mum used to go ‘primrosing’ to collect primroses where she grew up in Bath when she was a little girl, and now I go primrosing in the woods here in spring and deliver them to her,” Belles said.She added that her parents usually visited on Sundays for a roast, with her mother bringing pudding.What Savills said about the propertyVictoria Knight, head of office at Savills in Henley-on-Thames, described Blenheim Farm as a thoughtfully designed home that makes the most of its countryside setting.“Blenheim Farm has been thoughtfully designed to maximise its scenic setting and bring the outside in,” Knight said.She highlighted the floor-to-ceiling glass doors, light-filled living spaces, copper roll-top bath and colourful interiors, along with the property’s two kitchens, swimming pool, tennis court and games room.“With two kitchens, a swimming pool, tennis court and games room, this is a home perfectly suited to family life and entertaining on a grand scale,” Knight said.She also noted the property’s location along a quiet, tree-lined country lane, around 15 minutes from Henley.With an offer now accepted, the sale of Belles Berry’s South Oxfordshire mansion is progressing, according to the listing on Savills’ website.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: NMC asks Raj medical colleges to act swiftly on ragging complaints
articles.summary: NMC directs Rajasthan medical colleges to swiftly act on ragging complaints, protect confidentiality, prevent retaliation, and provide mental health support.
articles.body: Jaipur: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has directed medical colleges in Rajasthan to act promptly on ragging complaints and provide mental-health support to affected students after receiving eight complaints from the state in 10 days.The commission has instructed colleges to protect complainants’ confidentiality, as far as possible, and prevent retaliation, intimidation, isolation or pressure to withdraw complaints. It also directed institutions to address immediate safety concerns without waiting for inquiry reports to be completed.In a complaint involving Govt Medical College, Dausa, where students reported psychological distress, thoughts of self-harm or a risk of serious harm, NMC asked the college to arrange confidential assessment and support through qualified mental-health professionals. Institutions have also been asked to confirm that support measures have begun without unnecessarily disclosing sensitive medical information.In its letter to Dausa officials, NMC said, “Ensure that the complainant is protected from further contact, intimidation, threats, social boycott, or academic victimisation, as appropriate. Designate a responsible faculty member or nodal officer whom the student can contact confidentially. Ensure that no confrontation with the alleged perpetrators is forced upon the complainant.”Dr Rajendra Verma, principal of Govt Medical College, Dausa, said, “We have received the complaint and we will take the action accordingly. We will call a meeting of anti-ragging committee to find out the factual details. Those found guilty will be punished.”In a ragging complaint involving SN Medical College, Jodhpur, NMC sought details on whether anti-ragging helpline boards and grievance committees were functioning and prominently displayed in the college and hostels, as mandated by its public notice dated March 9, 2026. It also asked whether the Anti-Ragging Squad was conducting regular hostel inspections and what psychological counselling and safety assurances had been provided to the complainant.In a letter to Govt Medical College, Bhilwara, NMC noted that ragging complaints had been reported from the institution a few months ago and that it had earlier been advised to maintain zero tolerance. The commission said the latest complaint raised concerns over compliance with Supreme Court directions and NMC guidelines, as well as the functioning of the Anti-Ragging Committee, Anti-Ragging Squad and Hostel Committee.In the complaint concerning ESIC Medical College, Jaipur, NMC directed the authorities to ensure the immediate safety of the complainant and other affected students.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news.
